Fix an integer \(d\geq1\), numbers \(\alpha,\beta,L>0\), and known constants \(0<g_-<1<g_+<\infty\), all independent of the sample size. Put \(D=[0,1]^d\) and \(U=(-1,2)^d\).

For \(t>0\), set \(r_t=\lceil t\rceil-1\) and \(\eta_t=t-r_t\). Define \(\mathcal H^t(L)\) to consist of restrictions to \(D\) of functions \(f\in C^{r_t}(U)\) satisfying
\[
\sum_{|\nu|\leq r_t}\|D^\nu f\|_{\infty,U}
+\max_{|\nu|=r_t}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in U\\x\ne y}}
\frac{|D^\nu f(x)-D^\nu f(y)|}{\|x-y\|_2^{\eta_t}}
\leq L.
\]
Here \(\nu\in\mathbb N_0^d\) is a multi-index, \(|\nu|\) is its total order, \(D^\nu\) is the corresponding partial derivative, and \(\|h\|_{\infty,U}=\sup_{x\in U}|h(x)|\).

Let \(\mathcal P\) be the class of probability laws of \((X,A,Y)\) such that \(X\in D\) has an unknown Lebesgue density \(g\) satisfying \(g_-\leq g(x)\leq g_+\) almost everywhere, \(|A|,|Y|\leq1\) almost surely, and the conditional means admit versions
\[
a(x)=\mathbb E(A\mid X=x)\in\mathcal H^\alpha(L),\qquad
b(x)=\mathbb E(Y\mid X=x)\in\mathcal H^\beta(L).
\]
No regularity is imposed on \(g\), and the conditional joint law of \((A,Y)\) given \(X\) is otherwise unrestricted. From \(n\) independent observations with common law \(P\in\mathcal P\), the target is
\[
\psi(P)=\mathbb E_P\{\operatorname{Cov}_P(A,Y\mid X)\}
=\mathbb E_P(AY)-\int_D a(x)b(x)g(x)\,dx.
\]
Define the minimax squared-error risk
\[
R_n=\inf_{T_n}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}
\mathbb E_{P^{\otimes n}}\bigl[(T_n-\psi(P))^2\bigr],
\]
where the infimum is over all measurable estimators based on the observations; estimators may use the fixed class parameters but not the unknown functions \(a,b,g\).

Writing \(w=(\alpha+\beta)/d\), determine the unique ordered pair \((\gamma,\kappa)\), as a function of the fixed parameters and for all \(w>0\), such that
\[
\log R_n=-\gamma\log n-\kappa\sqrt{\log n}+O(\log\log n)
\qquad(n\to\infty).
\]
All logarithms are natural, and the implicit constant may depend on the fixed class parameters.
</problem>

24	## 1. Bounds that will be proved

44	## 2. Two polynomial facts
45	
46	Set
47	\[
48	l=g_-,\qquad h=g_+,\qquad
49	\rho=\frac{\sqrt h-\sqrt l}{\sqrt h+\sqrt l}.
50	\]
51	Thus \(0<\rho<1\) and \(c_g=\log(1/\rho)\).

53	### 2.1 Sharp approximation and moment annihilation
54	
55	With \(c=(h+l)/2\) and \(r=(h-l)/2\), the Chebyshev expansion is
56	\[
57	\frac1u=\frac1{\sqrt{lh}}
58	\left\{1+2\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}(-\rho)^j
59	T_j\left(\frac{u-c}{r}\right)\right\},
60	\qquad l\leq u\leq h.                                   \tag{3}
61	\]
62	Consequently, there are polynomials \(p_m\), of degree at most \(m\), such that
63	\[
64	\sup_{u\in[l,h]}|p_m(u)-u^{-1}|\leq C\rho^m.              \tag{4}
65	\]
66	
67	The matching dual identity is just as important. Define the signed measure
68	\[
69	\int F(u)\,d\sigma_m(u)
70	=\frac{(-1)^m}{\pi}\int_0^\pi
71	 F(c+r\cos t)\cos(mt)\,dt.
72	\]
73	For \(m\geq2\),
74	\[
75	\int u^j\,d\sigma_m(u)=0\quad(0\leq j<m),\qquad
76	\int\frac{d\sigma_m(u)}u=\frac{\rho^m}{\sqrt{lh}}.         \tag{5}
77	\]
78	Also \(\|\sigma_m\|_{\rm TV}\leq1\).

80	For completeness, (3) follows from
81	\[
82	\frac{1-\rho^2}{1+2\rho\cos t+\rho^2}
83	=1+2\sum_{j\geq1}(-\rho)^j\cos(jt)
84	\]
85	and the identities

87	c+r\cos t=\frac{\sqrt{lh}}{1-\rho^2}
88	(1+2\rho\cos t+\rho^2).
89	\]

92	### 2.2 Matrix versions with uniformly controlled derivatives
93	
94	We will use fixed-dimensional real symmetric matrices with eigenvalues in \([l,h]\). Formula (3), applied to a matrix, approximates its inverse.
95	
96	A slightly more general fact will be useful. A product of a fixed number of entries of inverses of such matrices has polynomial approximations \(Q_m\), of total degree at most \(m\), satisfying
97	\[
98	\|Q_m-Q\|\leq C(m+1)^b\rho^m,                            \tag{6}
99	\]
100	where \(b,C\) are fixed.
101	
102	These approximations also have a uniform analytic bound: on a fixed complex neighborhood of the allowed real matrices,
103	\[
104	|Q_m|\leq C\quad\text{for every }m.                      \tag{7}
105	\]
106	Here and below the matrix dimensions are fixed.
107	
108	Here are details ensuring that (7) does not hide a degree-dependent loss. Expand each inverse entry using (3), multiply the expansions, and retain terms whose total Chebyshev degree is at most \(m\). The discarded terms are bounded by
109	\[
110	C\sum_{j>m}(j+1)^b\rho^j
111	\leq C'(m+1)^b\rho^m.
112	\]
113	Choose \(1<R<1/\rho\). On a sufficiently small fixed complex neighborhood of the real symmetric matrices in question,
114	\[
115	\left\|T_j\left(\frac{G-cI}{r}\right)\right\|\leq C_RR^j.
116	\]
117	This follows from the matrix Cauchy formula on a Bernstein ellipse of parameter \(R\): the resolvents are uniformly bounded there. The multiplied series is therefore absolutely bounded by a convergent series with terms \(C(j+1)^b(\rho R)^j\). This proves (7).
118	
119	In particular, Cauchy estimates imply that for all \(s\geq0\),
120	\[
121	\frac1{s!}|D^sQ_m[z_1,\ldots,z_s]|
122	\leq C^{s+1}\prod_i\|z_i\|.                             \tag{8}
123	\]
124	The constants are independent of \(m\). The same conclusion holds after multiplication by any fixed-degree polynomial in bounded moment variables.
125	
126	## 3. An unbiased polynomial-estimation lemma
127	
128	We record the variance bound used for the upper bound.
129	
130	Partition \(D\) into \(k\) equal cubes of volume \(v=1/k\). In each cube, let \(Z\) be a vector of a fixed number of bounded local features of \((X,A,Y)\), multiplied by the cube indicator and divided by \(v\). Its mean \(\mu_C\) thus consists of normalized local moments.
131	
132	Suppose
133	\[
134	\Phi(P)=\sum_C vF_C(\mu_C),                               \tag{9}
135	\]
136	where each \(F_C\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(D_0\). Assume the \(F_C\)'s have a common bounded analytic extension to a fixed neighborhood of all their allowed moment vectors.
137	
138	Replace every product of \(j\) expectations in (9) by its unbiased average over \(j\) distinct observations. This defines a measurable unbiased estimator \(\widehat\Phi\). For \(D_0=O(\log n)\),
139	\[
140	\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\Phi)
141	 \leq \sum_{s=1}^{D_0}
142	 \frac{C^s k^{s-1}}{\binom ns}.                          \tag{10}
143	\]
144	Consequently,
145	\[
146	\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\Phi)
147	\leq \frac{CD_0}{n}
148	 \max\left\{1,\left(\frac{CD_0k}{n}\right)^{D_0-1}\right\}. \tag{11}
149	\]

153	\[
154	\frac1{s!}D^s\Phi(\mu)[Z_1,\ldots,Z_s].
155	\]
156	Before canonicalization this is zero unless all \(s\) arguments fall in the same cube. Bound (8), bounded features, and \(g\leq g_+\) show that its squared \(L^2\)-norm is at most \(C^sk^{s-1}\). 160	\binom ns^{-1}\leq \frac{2s!}{n^s},\qquad 1\leq s\leq D_0

174	k_j=2^{jd}

178	\theta_j=\langle\Pi_ja,\Pi_jb\rangle_g,\qquad

204	\]

209	\]

219	\frac{R_a^\top G^{-1}R_b}{\det(G_c)^2}.                 \tag{13}
220	\]

224	\frac{R_a}{\det(G_c)}

235	### 4.2 Polynomial approximation of the increment
236	
237	The matrix
238	\[
239	G^{-1}\det(G_c)^{-2}
240	=G^{-1}\{\det(G_c^{-1})\}^2
241	\]
242	has entries that are sums of products of \(2q+1\) inverse-matrix entries. Apply Section 2.2 and replace it in (13) by its degree-\(m\) polynomial approximation.
243	
244	The resulting approximation to the entire increment is a polynomial functional, of degree at most
245	\[
246	D_0=m+2q+2.
247	\]
248	By (6) and (14), its bias is bounded by
249	\[
250	Ck_{j-1}^{-w}(m+1)^b\rho^m.                             \tag{15}
251	\]
252	By (7), it satisfies the analytic boundedness assumption of Section 3, uniformly in \(m,j\). Hence it has an unbiased estimator with variance bounded by (10)–(11), using \(k=k_{j-1}\).
253	
254	The initial term \(\theta_0\) is handled directly by polynomial approximation of \(G^{-1}\). It has the same conclusions, with \(k=1\).
255	
256	We have proved the following usable construction:
257	
258	> At each resolution of complexity \(k\), an increment has an estimator with bias at most
259	> \[
260	> Ck^{-w}(m+1)^b e^{-c_gm},
261	> \]
262	> degree at most \(m+C\), and variance satisfying (10)–(11).

264	## 5. Upper bound below the elbow
265

267	\[
268	N=\log n,\qquad H=2\sqrt{c_gw(1-2w)}.
269	\]

271	\[
272	\delta=e^{-wN-H\sqrt N}N^M.                             \tag{16}
273	\]

276	k_J^{-w}\asymp\delta.
277	\]
278	
279	For an increment of complexity \(k\), including the initial term with \(k=1\), use

281	m(k)=
282	\left\lceil
283	\frac{wN+H\sqrt N-(M-A)\log N-w\log k}{c_g}
284	\right\rceil.                                         \tag{17}
285	\]
286	For all sufficiently large \(n\), these integers are positive and \(O(N)\).
287	
288	By (15),
289	\[
290	|\text{bias at this resolution}|
291	\leq C\delta N^{b-A}.
292	\]
293	There are \(O(N)\) resolutions. Taking \(A>b+3\), summing the biases, and using (12), gives total bias \(O(\delta)\).
294	
295	It remains to check the variances, including their leading stretched-exponential constant.
296

298	\[
299	D_0\leq
300	\frac{H\sqrt N-wx-(M-A)\log N}{c_g}+C.                  \tag{18}
301	\]
302	
303	If \(k\leq n/N^{B_0}\), with a sufficiently large fixed \(B_0\), then \(D_0\leq CN\) and the sharper part of (11) gives variance \(C/n=o(\delta^2)\).

308	\leq -N+O(\log N)+

310	\]
311	For \(-B_0\log N\leq x\leq0\), the last term is
312	\(O(\sqrt N\log N)=o(N)\), again giving \(o(\delta^2)\).

317	{4wc_g}.
318	\]

321	\frac{H^2}{4wc_g}N=(1-2w)N.                             \tag{20}
322	\]

325	Sum the increment estimators, and subtract the result from the empirical mean of \(AY\). The squared \(L^2\) triangle inequality costs at most the square of the number of resolutions. The empirical mean contributes \(O(1/n)\). Consequently,
326	\[
327	R_n\leq C N^{B}e^{-2wN-2H\sqrt N}.                      \tag{21}
328	\]
329	This proves the upper half of (1).

331	## 6. Upper bound at and above the elbow
332	
333	Suppose \(w\geq1/2\). Choose a sufficiently large fixed \(B_0\), and stop at a resolution satisfying
334	\[
335	k_J\asymp n^{1/(2w)}N^{-B_0}.
336	\]
337	Then
338	\[
339	k_J^{-w}\asymp n^{-1/2}N^{B_0w}.
340	\]
341	At complexity \(k\), choose
342	\[
343	m(k)=\left\lceil
344	\frac{\frac12N-w\log k+C\log N}{c_g}
345	\right\rceil,
346	\]
347	where \(C\) is large enough to absorb the polynomial factor in (15).
348	
349	All degrees are \(O(N)\), all resolutions satisfy \(k\leq n/N^{B_0}\) eventually, and their variances are \(O(1/n)\). The summed biases and the truncation error are \(n^{-1/2}\) times a fixed power of \(N\). Hence
350	\[
351	R_n\leq Cn^{-1}N^B.                                    \tag{22}
352	\]
353	
354	## 7. Lower bound below the elbow
355	
356	We now prove the lower half of (1). This also explains why the constant in (20) is sharp.
357	
358	### 7.1 Smooth regression bumps and irregular densities
359	
360	Use a partition into \(k=M^d\) equal cubes \(C_j\), and let \(\varphi_j\) be rescaled copies of a fixed nonzero \(C^\infty\) bump supported strictly inside each cube.
361	
362	For latent variables \(u_j\in[l_n,h_n]\) and signs \(R_j,S_j\in\{-1,1\}\), define
363	\[
364	a(x)=a_0k^{-\alpha/d}\frac{R_j}{u_j}\varphi_j(x),\qquad
365	b(x)=b_0k^{-\beta/d}\frac{S_j}{u_j}\varphi_j(x)
